## Intent
Hypothesis: fusing integrate+decide+respawn+render into a single register-only pass with no intermediate storage eliminates a second streaming pass and approaches the streaming ceiling.

## Layout & approach
The AoS layout offers 68 B/particle, of which the fused loop touches only 48 B (70% hot — age, color, pos, seed, vel); the remaining 20 B/p is dead weight dragged through every cache line. No intermediate storage means the death verdict stays in registers, halving nominal memory traffic versus a two-pass design. But the render stage performs a byte-granular read-modify-write scatter into the framebuffer — three or four RGBA channels per particle, each a load-add-clamp-store on a single byte — which introduces random-access stores that defeat streaming regardless of how few bytes the integration path touches. All measured N (10K–10M) sit past the L2 spill at N≈7710, so the working set is L3-resident or DRAM throughout.

## Cache saturation
Cost is flat to slightly *declining* across N within each death-rate band: at q=0.01, ns/p goes 26.1→25.9→25.4→24.2 from N=10K to 10M, actually improving as the working set moves from L3 to DRAM. There is no cache-spill knee at either the L2 or L3 transition. The dense grid confirms this: the algo is not bandwidth-limited, so larger working sets carry no penalty. Per-particle instruction overhead, not data movement, sets the cost.

## Bandwidth
Achieved bandwidth is 1.95–2.81 GB/s against the 12.69 GB/s ceiling — only 15–22% — and 4.5–6.5x above the 5.359 ns/p memory floor. This is overhead-bound, not bandwidth-bound. The algo runs 0.92–1.025x the naive scalar baseline at every N×q point: essentially identical to unoptimized scalar. Versus the winner (AF02.LP1-autovec.LP2-opt) it is 3.4x slower at q=0.01/N=10K, narrowing to 1.8x at q=0.5/N=1M — the winner's auto-vectorization advantage is largest at low death rates where compute dominates, while higher q adds respawn cost that partially equalizes but never closes the gap.

## Assembly
The codegen is scalar SSE with zero wide-vector instructions. The position integration uses 128-bit `vmovups`/`vmulps`/`vaddps` on xmm, but the render section is a byte-granular scatter repeated ~12 times: `movzx`+`add`+`cmp bx,0xff`+`cmovae`+`mov BYTE PTR` per channel, with bounds checks (`cmp r10,[rbp-0x40]`/`jae`) before each store. The 343-instruction body with 27 `cmp`, 11 `vucomiss`, 11 `jae`, and 7 `jne` explains the 63–67% frontend_stall: the instruction stream is too long and branchy for the frontend to supply, capping throughput far below the bandwidth ceiling despite branch_flush=0%.

## Verdict
Refuted — 0.92–1.025x of naive at every N×q point and 1.8–3.4x slower than the winner: the fused single-pass approach produces 343-instruction scalar codegen dominated by byte-granular framebuffer scatter (`movzx`/`add`/`cmovae`/`mov BYTE PTR`) and 63–67% frontend stalls, which cannot stream regardless of death rate or cache regime.
